title: Dennis Allen, Press Taylor, Richard Hightower on 'chasing greatness' | Press Conference
text: What was your assessment during the buy in terms of like self scouting? Things you like, things you want to improve on? >> Yeah, I think uh obviously take a look at the by-week and one of the main things that that we came away with. Obviously the guys are doing some things that are they're doing some things really well. Um and we can sit here and talk about all the great things that they done, but what we look at is the things that we can improve on because that's what where we want to take the next step. And coming out of the bye-week, we thought we had uh too many penalties. Um so that's an area that we addressed and uh you know, we got to get that stuff cleaned up because penalties equal field position and field position equals points. It's kind of how we see it. So um we're not uh in the top in the league in penalties. So we're near the bottom of the league, especially in penalties. But uh what is good for the group is they're one of the top ranked units in the league. Um, so if they just cut their penalties in half, I mean, they'll be uh where they really want to be. So that's what we're focusing on. Um, so and that's what I told the group. Hang on, Phil. That's what I told the group. So I told the group is exactly what I'm telling you guys. Hey guys, we got to clean up the penalties. All right. Um, bottom of the league in penalties, top in the league as a unit. Um, and that's even with all the horrible penalties that we have. So if we can get that stuff cleaned up, then you guys will really like the results. always focusing on the return game, proper hand placement, uh, and then the pre- snap penalties got to get cleaned up. >> What do you think was contributing to the penalties? I'm sure there's probably different reasons, but, uh, was a lot of it mental? >> No, I mean, some of them some of them have been, but it's a variation of different ones. Like, you have a couple where guys are out of position. Uh, so you're in bad position, you can't use the proper technique, and now you lunge and you reach and grab. So, um, one of the good things is in a return game, all right, in punt return and in kickoff return over the bye-week. We looked at they're top in the league in creating explosive plays. They're top in the league in explosives, what we consider explosives, but we also have given up too many things back. You know, we should have even more yards than we have now. So, we got a lot of explosives. All right, top in the league explosives, but the penalties make that average out where really um you want to be topping in the league in explosives, topping in the league in penalties. >> Steve, with the with DJ's penalty on the big Xavier, Richard, what was your assessment of that? >> Yeah, I mean, it is it is what it is. It's unfortunate that uh we don't get the touchdown there. It's unfortunate, you know. Um Xavier really wanted to put that ball in the end zone. He knew the goat was in the house. We all knew Hester was in the house. That's something Xavon dreams about doing is putting it in the end zone uh when Devin's there. So, um the positive about that is you take a look at it and you know we have the ability to do that. So, from now on, we just got to make sure we can control what we can control, get in the proper uh proper position with good body position, good leverage, pad under pad, hands inside, and do our best to work our technique. What have you >> and whatever happens from there happens from there. >> Sorry. What have you noticed with Brown their target? >> Say it again. >> Barry and Brown their >> I think he's good. I think he's dangerous player. I think when when given a seam he's explosive. Obviously, you know, um he had a lot of kick return touchdowns in college. He played with Zavon. He had five at Kentucky, five or six at Kentucky, one at LSU, and then Zavon obviously has some at LSU as well. But dynamic football player. I think he does a really good job. You talk about New Orleans, I mean, their unit, 44, Stalber, he's a good player. You know, he has 11 tackles on the year. He's their leading tackler. He's phenomenal. Um, Studsman, who I like coming out, number 28, uh, phenomenal linebacker. We'll see if he plays more defense or not now with, uh, Warner being hurt, with Pete being hurt, but, uh, I think he's a really good player for them as well. I think they got great speed on the outside with Styles, you know, and some of the perimeter speed they have outside is elite. They got 42 players out there um playing Gunner and playing Vice. So, we're going to have our work cut out for us. They do a good job. >> Coach, when the on the fake or the I'm sorry, the punt that got tipped. Um what when they overload to that side with that many guys? I mean, what I I sure limited in how you can answer this from a schemes perspective, but ju just I guess what went wrong there to prevent you guys having that totally covered on the left side? Yeah, I mean to be uh all transparency with you uh coach, like I don't I don't have a good bye-week because of that. Like, and then we in a race to get that fixed. It's happened twice now. We made some personnel adjustments. We made some schematic adjustments, but at the end of the day, like it's on me to get it corrected. So, it doesn't matter what happened on the field. I take accountability for whatever happens on the field. And I didn't I didn't have a very good bye-week because of it. So, um, and and I'm I'm going to get it fixed. We're going to get it fixed. >> Yeah. I mean, just working on trying to make sure we get things corrected because it's not a it's not a formula for winning football. Like, we can sit here and say we seven and two and pat ourselves on the back. That's not how our coaching staff operates. That's not how we operate. I can go in there and tell the players, you guys doing such a good job on this, this, and this. And we do tell them that, but my body weight operates from what's our motto is chasing greatness. So, we chase greatness every day. So, if it's not great and if it's not up to perfection, then that's what I want. So, my by-week doesn't look good when I don't feel like we can play as good as we're capable of playing. and we are playing good but I didn't I didn't like how we played the last game. >> You talk about fixing it [clears throat] you with with the players or can you elaborate on like how do you go about fixing that? >> Yeah, you just have to it's it's all about production. It's all about performing. So producing, right? So you go out there whatever we do we want to perform and produce. If we on kickoff coverage, we want to tackle the ball. And like you alluded to last week, Kyo's very good with net coverage or whatever the stat you were talking about. I don't even know all of those stats all the time that you come up with, but but it's true. He's he's top in the league in that. Okay. But what can we do better? We looking at the one play in Seattle where they got the ball past the 30 yard line, which we're not used to doing. So when they got to pass the ball past the 30 35 yard line, that's what I'm looking at. Um, I'm not looking at like all of the Attaba boys. We get those and we do those, but we chase we chasing greatness, man. We want to we want to be playing our best football in November and December, and we want to play in January, and we want to bring this we want to bring this city more hope and more joy. So, we we don't we don't pat ourselves on the back on on stuff that's happened in the past. We focus on New Orleans and the future and how we can get how we can get things done. So, that's just how I'm wired. This is how I operate. So, that's just that just is what it is. >> What did you think about the uh play the Seahawks made last week where they tipped the ball back to save it from going out of the end zone? >> Yeah, I thought it was awesome. It was unbelievable play. Obviously, Tory is not their primary returner. Um so, uh he uh he he did a a hell of a job, man, getting up there doing that. Obviously, you want to try to take the two-minute out of there, so he's trying to get it out the end zone. But I thought he I thought he did a great job. But doesn't surprise me. I mean, that kid that's a kid we went in I went and worked that kid out, spent a lot of time with his family and around him, and he is a he is so serious about football. Um that doesn't that doesn't surprise me about the way that he made that play. So again, outstanding job by him. And and then the one thing I do want to say uh before I leave because I probably be our last one there is I do want to give Cairo and the field goal unit uh a ton of credit because I as we talk about all the bad things or all the things that we feel like we can improve and correct if we take a look at that game. All right. And the object is to win the game, right? So the offense got us in a position to kick a game-winning field goal and those guys protected. Guy Daly did a great job with the snap. Tory did a great job with the hole and Cairo put it through the pipes and we got number seven. So now we're looking for number eight. So at the bottom of the at the end of the day, bottom line is winning the game and those guys found a way to win the game. So I'm proud of the field goal unit for that. >> Still kind of working through what life looks like with Jeffrey as part of your plan. But with the attention he commands, what has that done for you in terms of strategy and the creativity that come with your entire rush plan? >> Well, listen, I mean, I think anytime you have a player of that ability, you know, it allows you to do some different things and and certainly he's going to get a lot of attention, which is going to free up uh some things for some other people. So, I think as we continue to go along, we you know, you kind of have to see how your opponents are are treating that and what they're doing with that in terms of, you know, run game protection, those types of things. So, uh, [snorts] yeah, it it it, uh, it's a fun problem to have to try to figure out what the offense is going to try to do and then how can we try to attack that. [snorts] >> You've gotten him here, how has he raised the floor for what you guys are capable of doing with a four-man rush? Um, yeah, I think a lot of what we just talked about in terms of just like he commands a lot of attention, you know, and so, uh, with him commanding that much attention and it opens up, uh, some one-on-one opportunities for some other guys and and I think some other guys have benefited from that. So, uh, I think that's a positive thing that we have. I think, you know, the more really good players you have that have the ability to win their matchup, whether that's their matchup in coverage, their matchup, you know, in the run game, their matchup in the passing game. Uh, you know, winning these these one-on-one matchups are are are big in our league. And, uh, and so, um, you know, obviously when we can get him in a one-on-one, that's a great thing for us. And yet a lot of times the offense is going to give a lot of attention to him and and so some other guys are going to have to step up. >> As a play caller, what does it do for your job when you have you when you have your four guys up front? You don't have to necessarily rely on a blitz. Is that right or is that like a challenge? [clears throat] No, I think I think it um it allows you more flexibility in terms of how you can call the game, you know, um when you feel like um that you can get home with four, um then then that leaves you more flexibility. Whereas if if you don't feel like you can get home with four, you feel like ah I may have to bring a few more elements into the rush to try to affect the quarterback. So I just think it gives more flexibility to what we can do. didn't pop up in the injury report yesterday. Is there any concern or is he okay there? >> Uh yeah, I don't I don't anticipate any issues with him. Yeah. >> What do you think of his like his ability because his want to like challenging his teammates like telling my test, hey, if you get a one-on-one and a double me like >> Yeah, I think it's been awesome. I think it's been awesome. I think um you know when when you have really good players um that play at a certain effort level, they practice a certain way, they prepare a certain way. Um when you're that way yourself, it's easy to hold others accountable to that same standard. Um and so I think that's been I think that's been great uh for us. And and really honestly um when you get to that point when you have the more players that you have like that then it becomes a player-led group rather than a coachled group. Uh and that that's that's when you really have something special. >> We'll go right here to Larry. He's been waiting. >> Thank I appreciate that DA. I appreciate that. [laughter] >> Make it good. >> A lot of pressure you coached against Simmons. Um, obviously defense, defense, you [clears throat] watched him on tape, but now getting to work with him, like what has struck you about him as a person on and off the field. >> Yeah, listen, I mean, I I said that when we acquired him that, you know, part [clears throat] of the the the real intrigue about the player, I mean, obviously he's talented, uh, and he's been productive. Uh, but I think it's those intangible characteristics that make him even more important for our team and for our organization. um you know because uh you know I've been around some players that are really talented players and yet maybe their work ethic isn't quite what you want it to be and and that's really not the example that you want for the rest of the group and so uh again when your best players are your best workers um everybody else has to rise up to that level. [snorts] >> Do you think your defense needed a leader like him? Like was that missing? Um well to that maybe to that extent. Yeah. Um and yet look, we've always had a group of guys that come in and and and work um and do the things that they're being asked to do to to perform at a certain level. Um I think he just accentuates that. >> How have you seen Devin Bush take a step forward and especially over the last few weeks? >> Yeah, I think I think he's played at a high level the last few weeks. I think you know you know we've said this before. for I mean the thing that he really does well is is um man he can run you know and so when we can free him up and let him go run and hit run and cover do those types of things that's that's when he's uh at his best and and uh he's been able to do that the last couple of weeks >> can use his ability to he does so much like how would you characterize his value to to the defense >> man you know look we've talked a lot today about Jeffrey Simmons and and kind of the elite player. Um, but the best teams are made up of I call them role players. They know what their role is. They perform their role uh at a at a at a very high level and and that's that's what he does. I mean, he's a guy that when we brought him in here, we didn't bring him in here saying he's going to be the starter. uh we brought him in here because we felt like he could do multiple roles um and fill in in spots when needed to and we could still play at a high level on defense and and uh and I think that's important. You know, it's important. You're not going to have a team of a defense of an offense of uh 11 great players, elite players. Uh, but you can win a lot of games with a lot of really good players um that understand their role and can perform their role at a high level. >> That is to go back to the Tampa Bay game with Jaylen >> [snorts] >> um and the pick six kind of breaking that open. Was that like a long time coming for him or was there kind of a buildup to that moment? What allowed him to make that play? that I think it's just uh perseverance I guess like you know like just man it's a tough league that we're in you know and you just got to keep going out there and keep working uh and keep competing and that's what that's what he's done and he put himself in a good position he made a great play um got a light nice escort by Tez going down the sideline um and so yeah I mean look I think we were all excited to see that and and Um, you know, I'm anticipating more of that to come. >> On the note of On the note of Montes, I mean, I know he and Jeffrey played together in college. They're very close. He was mo he talked to us after the suspension, talked about how motivated he was to come in and prove, you know, prove his value again. Do you do you sense like that on almost like amplified Jeffrey's here and just that that's brought it differently? >> Yeah, I think that's fair. I think that's fair. I I think I think um you know coming back he was he was highly motivated um you know um you know sometimes you don't really know what you got until it's taken away from you know and so I think he was highly motivated already uh to come back and and perform well and and uh and I think you know adding adding Jeff to the mix uh has kind of accentuated that a little bit. Last three, Dan, Bill, and Dennis. With Carl Granderson, you obviously have unique insight. When he got to New Orleans, what was he and what have you made of what he's become now? >> And I I'm so proud of him. I mean, he he's uh look, we we uh we got him, you know, in the draft. I can't remember what round we got him in, but undrafted. Yeah. But I think we had like maybe third round grades on him. um you know and he had a he had an incident there that you know I think caused him to to go undrafted but u he he's you love those stories of guys that you know they they fight through adversity uh they get an opportunity they take advantage of that opportunity and the reason why he's taken advantage of that opportunity is because he's come in and worked his ass off to be that um he he he works hard he practices hard u he studies a game. Um and and and guys that do those things and have talent, which he does, they get better. And so, um yeah, I'm I'm I'm proud of him for what he's been able to accomplish. He's he's done a lot of good things. >> Uh DA, uh the Saints offensive numbers may not look pretty on paper, but it seems like they somehow find a way to points. Uh what do you see and how do you kind of gauge? >> Well, listen, I think they got explosive playmakers. Um, I think their skill position u is would would rank up there with with most uh of the good ones in this league. Um, you know, and so um I think they're they're one explosive play away from you know you know scoring points. So I think they're a dangerous team. Um they they they they've really been in every single game uh that they've that they've played in a majority of these other than two games I think Atlanta and Minnesota. All of them have end ended up being one-score games. Uh so they've put themselves in a in a position to win a lot of games and I this is a good football team we're playing, you know, and so uh we've got our work cut out. >> Uh Demarco Jackson, you know, from your time with him in New Orleans to what he's done now going from special teams to, you know, key player on defense, what have you seen in his growth? >> Uh yeah, I think he's he's he's grown a lot. I mean, you know, we talked about Carl Grannerson earlier. Demarco's really kind of the same way. You know, he's just a guy that comes in every day. Um, he goes to work. Uh, he's got a business-like approach. Um, he studies the game and he's been prepared and ready to go every time that we've we've called on him. So, uh, he's a he's a big part of what we do. I know what uh well we all know what Cole Kit has meant a lot on the field, but are there like intangible differences that you see now that you don't have him? >> Yeah, I definitely I mean there's there's a void in leadership obviously when Cole's not around Cole he was a guy when we got here we were told about the leadership abilities and things like that. He's a guy that last year as guys are learning a system as guys are learning the expectations of a new coaching staff and what the standard is he was a guy we could lean on for that. Um, so there's certainly a void when you take a guy like that out of out of the building. Um, not just out of the huddle, not out of the locker room. He's not in the building right now, so when he gets back around, we're all looking forward to that. I know guys reach out to him, keep in touch with him a lot. Um, but there's certainly an opportunity for guys to step forward and kind of take on that leadership role. Um, just from the things that we're missing from Cole because he was such an integral part of what we're doing, what we're building here. >> How big of a boost is it to get the young guy back? >> Uh, hopefully that's a a great boost for us. We'll see where he's at in terms of of playing and his availability, but you know, just adding another talented back to the room, the ability to kind of have that two-headed monster with both those guys in there splitting carries, splitting time, just changing the presentation to the defense. So, we're excited about the progress that that Kyle's made and see where he's at moving forward. >> As an extent of the Phil's question, Sam Robs has seen his role increase with with Co., where is he now compared to his first few weeks in terms of mastering the offense, knowing his assignment out there and doing what he needs to do? >> Yeah, he's doing a great job getting better. I mean obviously you would you would expect that from week one, week two to week 10 now. Um just understanding the rhythm of the week, what it looks like, understanding the expectation on each and every play, maybe even us understanding what his skill set is and putting him positioned to do what he does well and where he thrives right now, understanding the matchups, but there there obviously is more on his plate now with uh you know, everybody kind of moves up the dep chart when you take Cole out of the equation there. So he's a guy we've leaned on. He's a guy that's been been producing and continuing to progress. And so that's something now you're kind of at the point in the season there's no rookies anymore. You know, guys have played enough, guys have enough exposure, guys have practiced enough to where we expect you to kind of move on and graduate from rookie mistakes and things like that. And that that's something we're encouraged with what we've seen from Sam, but we obviously expect to continue to see progress from her. >> Russ, on the topic of of run game efficiency, what's your process of u judging it, I guess, whether it's measuring it statistically or or just using the eye test? >> Um, I mean, really statistically, we kind of do. It's it's really 40% on first down. So, whatever that being first and 10, typically four yards is explosive, half on second and then converting on third down. Now, we understand too there's times on third down where you're we're almost setting up fourth down at certain times. Where it gets skewed is when you get into situational numbers. Third and one, gain it. So, one yard runs an efficient run. The red zone obviously that changes too, cutting things in half. But that's kind of where we go from there. But I think too like the eye test just seeing what it looks like. Are the fundamentals techniques showing up? Are we rolling off the ball? Are our eyes, our tracks, the fundamentals of fundamentals of blocking, the fundamentals of um the discipline of the running backs, the tracks, the landmarks, the eyes, the vision, the explosion, the cut, all those types of things are things that we try to evaluate each and every time. Are there certain schemes that we're better at that we see better? Are there certain matchups that we get more out of? Things like that. Um, as you go and you evaluate, but it's certainly something we feel like we get a little bit more out of. So, what did the bye-week tell you guys needs to be emphasized with the run game to get the efficiency where you want it? >> Really, honestly, probably a recommitment to our fundamentals and techniques, and that's from everybody. That's the way we run off the football. That's the way our hat placement, our hand placement, our backside hand, the tracks of the backs, the finish of the quarterback a lot of times in the run game. He he's an integral part of that. Um, so so just kind of reinvesting in what we believed in in training camp and started the season with and now we get a chance to step back, breathe a little bit. Are are we getting exactly what we thought we'd get and hoped we'd get? Can we recommit to some of these things and and dive in a little bit more? >> Earlier, uh Ben was talking about uh the the opponent's pass rushing allowing too many free runners to the AMB gaps. Is that a setting up protection issue, knowing assignments or technique? What's leading to that? >> Uh there's been a number of different things whe whether it's I mean it's really kind of a case by case basis. Sometimes it's movement um post snap from a defensive line that causes somebody's eyes to be in the wrong place potentially. Um sometimes like we talked about in the run game, there could be a technique issue in the way we we approach a block. Um but we want to be definitive. We want to be decisive. We want to make sure we are coaching each protection. We're crystal clear with the expectations, the rules, the progression based on the looks we're getting. Um so it's something that we feel like, you know, if there's something that's a reoccurring issue, we need to invest our time in it. We need to put it make it a point of emphasis to get that thing cleaned up because in this league if there's blood in the water you're going to continue to see the same things over and over and over. >> Like the Saints pass rush is their best thing that they do on defense especially their ends. Do you agree with that? And how good are they? What makes them so good? >> Yeah, I agree with that. And obviously, you know, they like to kind of run the backers through the the the interior gaps as well. So that kind of thins your line out at times, creates a dent in it. You end up in one-on-one situations and they're these are good pass rushers. I mean, Chase Young obviously has a reputation for that. Granderson has done a great job this season. I think both those guys are up around eight sacks. So, you know, it's the added element of pressure and then it's just talented pass rushers to begin with. So, they do a good job and then the coverage element of starting in shell and rotating late kind of causes the quarterback to hold the ball. The pockets collapsing. You can see why they're effective with what they're able to do. >> I'm curious what your perspective on like Caleb started out super hot last week and then the interceptions get like what what did you why do you from your perspective why do you think that happened? >> Um, you know, I don't know. I I think part of it we're in a sec we're in a situation I think we were going to be second and four on at the four yardd line second goal at the four yard line all of a sudden we're in a penalty second 21 I think that was probably a decision he'd like to have back the first interception I think there were two that were he's trying to throw the ball away and we got to make sure that it's clear and obviously thrown away you know we can't leave it in harm's way in there and then another one I think was a one-on-one situation ball got knocked up in the air and got intercepted so I don't know that it's any now the the first one I would say the decision alone and he understands that talking through the concept what we're looking for where we want to go with the ball. I think maybe that was it's a second long trying to get a little bit more than we needed on that particular situation. Other ones are just, you know, we can't leave the ball on the field of play or we can't leave it up to chance whenever we're trying to get rid of the ball in a muddy pocket situation. >> When you see something like that, do do you change at all what you guys are doing to try to get get him back in rhythm or is it just still what usual? >> Um, I don't know. It's kind of a quarterback. You kind of one of the things you always ask for as a play caller, you know, what's the look in his eyes? Does he look shaken by this? That's not something you've seen from Caleb. So, it's something we're going to keep firing. Um, if it was a reoccurring issue over, we're missing this coverage, you know, we're missing the coverage tail, whatever it is. We're being tricked by things. That would be a different discussion. Um, leaving the ball on the field to play in some throwaway situations or or near enough to defenders make a play on it. That's another thing that, you know, we believe we'll be able to correct moving forward as well. How much has that trust in him grown that he doesn't get shaken by those things? >> Yeah, I mean, you've seen it continuously like that's something that's been his thing, you know, late in last year, you think of kind of the the late game plays he's able to make things like that. He um he's demonstrated that over and over. So, as you see it over and over over and continue to reveal itself, then you're going to trust him more and more with that type of situation. Um, and every game is really a learning opportunity for all of us to learn how everybody responds to certain situations, uh, as a unit, as an individual, whatever that may be. >> How did you evaluate Azie at the buy? Just the situation at left tackle right now. Is it simply that Theo is playing really well and you don't feel like you need to make a switch there or is Aussie just not ready to handle a full game load just? >> Um, you know, I think that's kind of something we'll continue to evaluate as the season goes. each and every week we're looking through it. How practice goes through the week. We put a put a huge emphasis on that as well. Um I think we've been pretty pleased with what Theo has given us at this point in time, but it's something, you know, that's it's still a week by week. It's something that we there's been certain weeks we have a plan to rotate as a game goes. Um and so that's just something we'll continue to look at move forward. >> Talked about the void, the leadership void with Cole, but how have you seen the void of Cole in the run game and run blocking and have you guys had to make adjustments? It's not necessarily so easy to be like next man up when you're talking about what kind of blocker Cole was. >> Yeah, that's that's a great thing. Um it's really, you know, you go into every game with a plan of how you want to be the how you can be the most effective running the ball, throwing the ball, passing the ball, whatever that may be. Um and so, you know, you're taking Cole's obviously he was a he's a great pass protector. We felt like he does a great job on the front side and the backside in the run game. So you're trying to supplement those situations, whether it be with Sam, Steve, Cole, Coloulston, whether a jumbo tight end. There's certain looks. So it certainly changes your complexion based on your personnel and how you deploy everybody to put them in the best possible situation, but um it's just like anything, who's available, how are we going to do this, and so it changes week to week based on who's up, who's not. Cole's obviously not with us right now, so just continue to try to move forward with that. >> How has he grown as a past? Um, I think he's got a better understanding of his balance and keeping his base underneath him, not being so topheavy leaning forward in certain situations. Um, and really just understanding the spot, the launch point of the quarterback, the timing of the quarterback. That's a big part of things. Do I need to take the air out of the pass rusher? What type of pass am I playing against? I think all that experience just kind of lends you to be a little bit more confident, maybe even add to your repertoire of how I'm going to set certain guys uh throughout the course of a game early on, change the looks, things like that. So, I think you're just seeing growth from a player that's getting a chance to play more and more. >> Before Caleb got hurt, we were talking with you just about like his legs being a weapon. That might be something you want to tap into. And I know earlier this week he said that, you know, maybe the lack of running is busy hasn't needed to. How do you how how do you have to be mindful about making sure that that's not something that can reagravate the injury, but also knowing that eventually you might want to tap into that as a resource on offense. title: Chairman and CEO, Clark Hunt Speaks on New Stadium Updates and the 2026 NFL Season
text: All right. Good morning, everybody. Thank you all for being here. I want to start off with a few comments about the season to this point. Overall, I'm really pleased with the team's performance to this stage. Obviously, last year was tough, but I feel like the team came into training camp with the right mindset and that that's carried over into the season. It's been great to see Patrick Mahomes looking like Patrick Mahomes, and it's been really exciting to see some of the new players like Kenneth Walker. One of the more impressive things has been the production and development of the young players. My hat goes off to Andy Reid and Brett Veach for the [clears throat] job they've done in bringing those players in and coaching them up. We have a long way to go, and I know that we're going to have to continue to improve, but I've really enjoyed watching the team compete every week. On the stadium front, obviously yesterday was a really big day as the lease documents were approved between the Chiefs and the Kansas Sports Facilities Authority. The KSFA had its first meeting yesterday in Topeka, and we look forward to what I know will be a long and productive relationship with them. In the same vein, I want to thank Governor Kelly, Lieutenant Governor Toland, Mayor Watson, Mayor Bacon, and the other civic leaders in the state of Kansas who have helped make this opportunity a reality. This has truly been a team effort, and I want to extend my gratitude to everyone involved. We are committed to creating an incredible experience for Chiefs fans, and I'm excited to be able to report that there's a lot of momentum on the project. And with that, I'll open it up. >> On the stadium, this is obviously an incredibly expensive to build and and operate and so on. How important is it for you to have the families that have been coming to this stadium for generations to be able to afford that experience in the new stadium? >> Yeah. That's obviously an important consideration. We want to build off the tradition and legacy that we've had here at Arrowhead and a big part of that is our fan base. And you know, we're very hopeful that the fans who've enjoyed coming to Arrowhead for decades will be able to to come to the new facility in Kansas. >> We haven't made a firm consider firm decision on that, but it's definitely under consideration. >> [clears throat] >> Because if we were going to sell PSL's, we we had to factor that into the documents. >> And then community impact agreement, what community leaders did you have at the table >> Those discussions were really with the state of Kansas. That was something that was very important to the lieutenant governor. And he made sure that we we had a robust community impact agreement. >> Yeah, none of the documents yesterday had an exact location of where the stadium's going to be built. Are you able to share exactly where it will be? >> We're not 100% there yet. We we at this point have probably 98% of the property under contract. It's in Wyandotte County close to the Kansas Speedway. >> The the political dynamics in the state of Kansas right now are really interesting with Governor Laura Kelly being done with David Toland soon in two months. And then you have a governor coming in and Cindy Holshue who actually voted against the ownership bill that the legislature passed back in March. So things took a big step forward yesterday. Have you guys had any conversations with the incoming governor because she was opposed to the ownership structure of the bill that passed this past session? >> We've not had any conversations with the incoming governor. We look forward to doing so. Our been our focus has been on getting the uh documents done uh here with the lieutenant governor and governor Kelly. >> Todd, couple things on the state you shared some more more pictures yesterday. And how close are you to kind of [clears throat] really final designs? I mean these things just about exactly what it's going to look like? >> I I would say they're they're probably at 80 90% uh completion at this point from a conceptual standpoint. Um we'll have more renderings that we'll be able to share in the spring as as the design gets closer to final. >> And it looks like you know you have the see-through ceiling but for basketball looks like there's some sort of covering on there. Is this kind of a first of its kind thing? Can you take us through maybe the idea there? >> Yeah. Well one one of the considerations uh on an event like the NCAA Final Four is making sure the lighting's right. So we've looked at uh different ways that we can control the lighting uh in a building that that is going to have a roof that's going to allow a lot of light in. >> Is that something that's been done somewhere else? >> I don't I don't think it's been done on a uh year-round basis. I think on a temporary basis uh some arenas have done that. >> Nick. >> Yeah. Clark, when you [clears throat] look back at the 2012 to where you guys are now with the Super Bowls, with what you and Andy have built and then to where you going to be with the stadium, kind of what do you reflect on with all that? >> Um well one [clears throat] of the things that I'll take away from the last decade is what a special time this has been uh for the Chiefs organization and really our uh entire fan base. Obviously, Andy Reid deserves a lot of the credit for that, Brett Veach, the amazing leaders that we've had on the team, guys like Travis Kelce and Patrick Mahomes. And in in some ways the success that we've had over the last decade has really helped lay the foundation for this opportunity. And I think everybody who's been part of the organization over that time period has had a hand in creating this opportunity. >> Clark, you mentioned this a bit earlier about so many young players and players particularly that were selected late in the draft and helped this team win this year. What to say about Brett that he found those players? [clears throat] Well, we walked out of the draft this past April feeling like you know he had done it again, right? If you think back to the 2022 draft when when we really got a bunch of players who played a key role in a couple of those Super Bowl victories, the feeling inside the building was certainly that you know we had chosen some good players again and it's been really gratifying to see them excel on the field in in their rookie year. We're one of the youngest teams in the National Football League and for us to have success not only this year but in the years to come, you know we need those guys to be able to produce. >> Clark, on a different subject, you guys made the decision to bring Justin Tucker in and add him to the mix. He had 60 allegations, [snorts] did not appeal his suspension. A lot of you know you mentioned the fans about the stadium and having that in your consideration. What was your consideration towards the fans' reaction and did you play a role in that signing? Were you consulted on that? Did you have an input on that? >> Yeah. Brett and I did talk about it before he moved forward. certainly we take the allegations uh very seriously. We do not condone that type of behavior at all. We we like the fact that it was 10 years ago um and that he had served his suspension and some of the research that we did on him really got us to a point where we were comfortable giving him a second chance. Um and at the end of the day he was brought in to to create a little bit of depth for our special teams. >> Do you have just a Do you have a policy that you give to Brett and Andy as far as players and and behavior? Is there a line that that can't be crossed when it comes to players? >> I I think each situation is specific and you just got to talk about about the details. Um and that is something that that we do periodically when there are players that that have issues like like Kareem Hunt the the [clears throat] last couple of years. >> [snorts] >> Um do you have any thoughts on what happens at Arrowhead when you guys are gone? >> You know we really don't. It it belongs to the county and that's really going to be up to them to make a decision on it. >> You know as you think about the stadium in 2030 Brett and Andy are signed through 29. Um do you do you have any thoughts about I mean Andy of course is not going to go forever. Brett's a little bit younger. Do you have any thoughts about the future beyond that to Andy? >> Yeah. [clears throat] Well we would obviously like to keep that leadership team together as long as we possibly can. I'm I'm hoping that Tammy Reid will let Andy you know stay with us a a little bit longer and certainly you know hope Brett will want to continue to be with the Chiefs as well. >> The the politician's perspective on the stadium discussion is is interesting. I asked about incoming governor Cindy Holshul on the Kansas side. Jackson County future executive Stacy Lake has even tried to keep you guys at Arrowhead. And uh the Sports Authority is is really the landlord uh for the stadiums and so that's who we work most directly with. >> Last one, Todd. >> Clark, another off-the-field thing. It I know you guys try to educate guys on financial stuff. I know the union tries to, the NFL does. Is that responsibility basically end up with the the player on some of those things or what what what hand can you guys have in making sure guys financial decisions and the other decisions? >> Yeah. Uh the NFL has a great partnership with the Players Association from an education standpoint and it seems like every couple of years uh that education program uh becomes more robust. Um and uh you know, I'm I'm aware of the training that that they go through and we certainly have resources that are available uh to players uh on a whole whole lot of issues including financial. And so at the end of the day, it's their responsibility, but I do think the education part of it's really important. >> Thanks, Clark. Clark.

title: Christian Parker considered leaving Cowboys; Aikman-Buck feud + Week 11 nuggets | PFT PM (FULL)
text: PFCPM Thursday edition week 11 is already here. The nuggets are coming up. That is the factual information that comes from the NBC Sports Research document that comes out every Wednesday. I take a look through it. I pull out anything that I think is interesting to me and I hope that it ends up being interesting to you. Couple of interesting topics before we get to the Nuggets. And Christian Parker spoke today. He's the Dallas Cowboys defensive coordinator who is no longer calling the plays. And it was clear from his comments that he considered resigning after he learned that the most important aspect of his job would no longer fall within his job duties. And he ultimately decided to stay put. He said he didn't want to run from it. He was asked if it would be awkward. It's only awkward if we allow it to be awkward, he said. And it's hard not to look at this and say, "Did Jerry Jones simply not want to owe his buy out? Is it that simple?" Because you can move on from a coach at any time. You just have to pay him the balance of whatever is left on his contract. And we have seen in the past that there will be a coach who stays all the way through the end of the contract in Dallas and then once there is no further financial obligation, that's when a change is made. And of course, this comes in the aftermath of the observation that paying for coaches and getting performance by way of wins. There's no connection. And I think he even realized that that is not factually accurate. And it doesn't take much research to prove that there is a connection between how much you're paying for coaches and how much you win. But I fall back to the days when I used to practice law. And in a situation like this, Christian Parker comes into the office and says, "This is what they've done. This is my job. They've taken away my most important job duties. Everything I else everything else I do is just the precursor to what the defensive coordinator does on game day. I call the plays for the defense. And it's even more important in a team where the head coach is an offensive specialist. This isn't Shawn Payeyton taking the play calling duties away from the offensive coordinator. This is the head coach or whoever made the decision reassigning Christian Parker's duties to an assistant who was just hired a month ago to come in and help them fix the defense. And we broached the topic earlier today on PFT Live as to whether or not Mike Pentton's part of the problem. He's been there for a month. He's had a chance to try to make this defense better. And I guess we should have always seen in hindsight where this was going. Pent comes through the door. He's around for a few weeks. If the defense doesn't significantly improve, then he ends up calling the defensive plays. You have someone in house that you can turn to if you decide that you don't want to allow Christian Parker to call the plays. But if he'd seek out my advice and I was still practicing law, the first thing I'd say is, "Let me see your contract." Because there are certain duties that if you take them away from the employee, you've essentially fired that person, it's called a constructive discharge. You have changed the job so dramatically that the job is no longer the job anymore and the effort is just to get you to leave. You have dramatically changed the job. And even beyond whether or not it rises to the level of constructive discharge, the contract may spell out that this is what the job includes. Now, it comes down to what the standard language is that the Cowboys use, how much haggling was done over what about this line, what about that line, what about this, what about that. The Cowboys would want to have full flexibility to change any and all assignments for Christian Parker whenever they see fit. But at some point it strikes to the heart of what your job is. You've hired me to be the defensive coordinator. And again, I'd want to look at the full contract. I'd want to see what it says, what it doesn't say about play calling duties and the possibility that those things will be reassigned without affecting the employment obligations. Because there could be an argument to be made. No, you've essentially fired me and you want me to just hang around or you're hoping that one of these days I'll just say I can't keep doing this. This is too awkward. There's no way to make this unawward. I'm the defensive coordinator and I'm not calling the plays. Why am I even here on game day? Mike Pton's the one who's running the show on game day. I run the show the rest of the week. I don't run the show on game day. And then the next question becomes, is he really the defensive coordinator or are they just leaving the title on him? That would be another question under the contract and the facts involved. Had they essentially made Mike Pton the defensive coordinator and demoted Christian Parker to whatever it is he's going to be doing moving forward. because at some point you'd want to be able to make the argument that I shouldn't have to stay. You've essentially fired me. You've fired me and you're hiding behind labels and technicalities to force me to keep showing up because you don't want to pay my buyout. So, every day that he walks through the door, he's undermined. He's working a job that he didn't take when he was hired. And it just creates a bad situation. If you're trying to turn the team around, why do you even want to invite that complexity into your locker room? If he's just gone, he's gone and we move forward. But he's still there, but he's not calling the plays. And Mike Pentton's running the show. and you have mixed signals being sent to your players and you may have some players who are still upset and maybe they're more inclined to listen to Christian Parker or other players who are gravitating toward Mike Pton. You get divisions that way. I just don't think it's good for the overall team chemistry that you're trying to build. I think the easiest thing to do in a situation like that if you decide that the defensive coordinator isn't getting it done, you just move on and whatever cost it costs, it's a sunk cost, you just move on. But it's instructive to the way that Jerry Jones views the coaching staff. And that's why when people talk about Brian Shottenheimer being on the hot seat, the first question I want to ask, how much longer is he guaranteed to be paid? Sometimes these contracts don't have guarantees all the way to the end. I remember when Rex Ryan was getting toward what would have been a lame duck year back when the NFL teams seemed to not want a coach to work as a lame duck. He was heading toward the lame duck year, so he got a new contract, but it only guaranteed him the upcoming year and one more year. So after that season, the Jets decided to fire him, they only owed him one more year, not the balance of the deal. So when Brian Shottenheimimer, who was surely appreciative to have any head coaching offer some 15 years after the window by all appearances closed on his brief time as a candidate, if the deal breaker was 3 years of full guarantee versus two years of full guarantee, at some point you're just going to say fine, just whatever it takes to get the job. So, if he only had two years of full guarantee, far more likely that he could be on the outs. If he has a third year that is fully guaranteed based upon what we know of the aversion to buying out coaches and owing anyone money to not work, that could end up being a situation where Brian Shottrubber gets another season. And it all comes back to that fundamental question. How much are you willing to pay for your coaches? How much money are you willing to spend on the side of the business that isn't constrained by a salary cap or governed by a salary floor that you can spend as much or as little as you want on your coaches and you can avoid a buyout and still find something for Christian Parker to do that you otherwise would have to hire someone to do or push tasks on to others, but you're going to get value for this contract. Nobody's getting a free ride. Nobody's getting paid to not work. Is that really good for the Cowboys? I don't think it is. And we'll find out when the season ends. If the Cowboys continue on this trajectory where they don't make it to the playoffs, and right now it looks like they won't. What will happen the day after? The most important nugget in all of that is whether or not Brian Shottenheimimer's contract guarantees his pay for 2027. If it does, he's less likely to be gone. If it doesn't, you're probably going to see a new head coach in Dallas come 2027. text: a three-time Super Bowl champion, a three-time first-team all-pro player, and a seven-time pro bowler. In other words, he's going to the Hall of Fame one day, too. His name is Chris Jones. We always emphasize our goals and the leaders do a great job of, you know, staying committed to those goals throughout the year, no matter the circumstances. So I think there's a reiteration process that goes on throughout the year of what's important and how we're going to get there. >> Who reiterates it? How often >> Of course, it's a standard, you know. We were just having this conversation in the D-line room and, you know, Reed was like it starts up front and you know me and Joe was joking about it. When doesn't it start up front? He doesn't look 35 years old. >> Isn't that amazing what he's Listen, again, you know, I I know you you obviously have your own standard, um, but I'm just wondering what it looks like to you when you're watching it, that it's amazing, right? >> I'm amazed.
